summary: This dissertation develops resonator-based readout techniques for floating-electron qubits on cryogenic substrates (liquid helium and solid neon) and demonstrates a low-power cryogenic microwave source. Three main experimental systems are demonstrated: RF reflectometry detection of Rydberg transitions on helium achieving $0.34$ aF/Hz capacitance sensitivity, NbTiN superconducting nanowire resonators for electrons on neon with $Q_\mathrm{int} \approx 2.3 \times 10^5$, and a $140$ MHz tunnel-diode oscillator consuming $1$ μW for scalable qubit readout.
motivation: Floating electrons on cryogenic substrates offer exceptionally long predicted coherence times (spin $T_2 \sim 100$ s on helium, $\sim 0.1$ ms on neon) and promise scalable quantum computing with high-density qubit packing. However, practical readout and control electronics for such systems remain underdeveloped, particularly for integration with superconducting resonators and cryogenic signal sources.
method: For helium experiments, a high-Q LC tank circuit ($Q \sim 311$ at $121.9$ MHz) with Corbino-plate capacitor was integrated with a microfabricated Nb spiral inductor; Rydberg transitions were detected via frequency-modulated microwave irradiation combined with RF reflectometry. For neon experiments, NbTiN nanowire resonators ($4.81$ GHz, $20$ nm film on Si) were deposited with solid neon and electrons; theoretical analysis predicted spin-photon coupling and gate fidelities using integrated cobalt micromagnets. A tunnel-diode oscillator with varactor-tuned LC circuit was characterized at millikelvin temperatures for phase noise and amplitude stability.
result: Helium readout achieved single-electron sensitivity ($60$ aF expected for nanoscale devices, $0.34$ aF/Hz demonstrated), sufficient for future qubit detection at $10$ mHz bandwidth. Neon resonators maintained $Q_\mathrm{int}$ on order $10^5$ after neon/electron deposition; theoretical analysis predicts single/two-qubit gate fidelities approaching $99.99$%/$99.9$% with natural neon. TDO achieved $-115$ dBc/Hz phase noise at $1$ MHz offset, outperforming CMOS at $4$ K in mid-frequency range, with superior amplitude stability compared to commercial sources.
